section.title: A Call for Justice, Not Empty Fasting
section.sectionRationale: Two years after the night visions, a delegation asks whether they should keep fasting over the fall of Jerusalem. God answers with a searching question: was your fasting ever really for Me? He recalls the earlier prophets who called for justice and mercy, and the hard hearts that ignored them and were scattered. Ritual without a heart for justice is worthless.
section.thesis: God does not want religious ritual performed for ourselves; He wants true justice, mercy, and compassion flowing from a soft heart, for the earlier generation's refusal to do justice, not their neglect of fasting, is what brought the exile.
section.frameNote: Three movements: the delegation's question about fasting; God's probing of self-centered ritual and His summons to the words of the earlier prophets; and the ancient call to true justice, met by hard hearts, resulting in the scattering that made the pleasant land desolate.

verses.text: In the fourth year of King Darius, the word of the LORD came to Zechariah on the fourth day of the ninth month, the month of Chislev.
Now the people of Bethel had sent Sharezer and Regem-melech, along with their men, to plead before the LORD
by asking the priests of the house of the LORD of Hosts, as well as the prophets, “Should I weep and {{tsum|fast}} in the fifth month, as I have done these many years?”
Then the word of the LORD of Hosts came to me, saying,
“Ask all the people of the land and the priests, ‘When you fasted and mourned in the fifth and seventh months for these seventy years, was it really for Me that you fasted?
And when you were eating and drinking, were you not doing so simply for yourselves?
Are these not the words that the LORD proclaimed through the earlier prophets, when Jerusalem and its surrounding towns were populous and prosperous, and the Negev and the foothills were inhabited?’”
Then the word of the LORD came to Zechariah, saying,
“This is what the LORD of Hosts says: ‘Administer true {{mishpat|justice}}. Show {{chesed|loving devotion}} and compassion to one another.
Do not oppress the widow or the fatherless, the foreigner or the poor. And do not plot evil in your hearts against one another.’
But they refused to pay attention and turned a stubborn shoulder; they stopped up their ears from hearing.

They made their hearts like flint and would not listen to the law or to the words that the LORD of Hosts had sent by His Spirit through the earlier prophets. Therefore great anger came from the LORD of Hosts.
And just as I had called and they would not listen, so when they called I would not listen, says the LORD of Hosts.

But I scattered them with a whirlwind among all the nations that they had not known, and the land was left desolate behind them so that no one could come or go. Thus they turned the pleasant land into a desolation.”

tsum.gloss: To fast, to abstain from food as an act of mourning, repentance, or seeking God. The people had fasted for seventy years to mourn the temple's destruction. God's question is not whether fasting is good but whether their fasting was ever truly directed to Him or was really a self-focused ritual, exposing the difference between outward observance and a heart turned to God.

mishpat.gloss: Justice, judgment, the right ordering of society according to God's standard, especially the fair treatment of the vulnerable. True mishpat is not merely correct legal procedure but active, faithful dealing that protects the weak. God summarizes the message of the earlier prophets as a call to render true justice, the very thing the exiles' ancestors refused to do.

chesed.gloss: Loving devotion, steadfast love, covenant kindness and mercy. It is the loyal, generous love God shows His people and calls them to show one another. Paired with compassion, it moves beyond bare justice to warm-hearted care for the neighbor, the widow, the orphan, the foreigner, and the poor, the fruit God desires far more than ritual.

basic.context: Two years after the night visions, a delegation from Bethel comes to ask the priests and prophets whether they should keep fasting in the fifth month to mourn Jerusalem's fall. God answers with a question of His own: in all those seventy years of fasting, was it really for Me, or for yourselves? He then recalls the message of the earlier prophets, a call to true justice and mercy that the pre-exile generation refused, which is why God scattered them and left the land desolate.
basic.hermeneutics: This is prophetic teaching in response to a real question. God does not simply say yes or no about fasting; He redirects the whole issue to the heart. The point is timeless: religious ritual done for our own sake, without justice and mercy, is worthless to God. The history of the hard-hearted ancestors is a warning to the returned community not to repeat their sin.
basic.originalLanguages: Their practice was the tsum, the fast of mourning, kept for seventy years. God's real desire is mishpat, true justice, the right treatment of the vulnerable, joined with chesed, loving devotion, covenant kindness and mercy to one another. The earlier generation refused these, making their hearts like flint, and so were scattered.
basic.typology: The prophetic call to justice over empty ritual runs straight to Jesus, who quoted the prophets, I desire mercy and not sacrifice, and who denounced religion that neglects justice, mercy, and faithfulness. The hard heart of flint anticipates God's promise of a new heart, fulfilled by the Spirit in the new covenant.
basic.christ: Jesus stands squarely in this prophetic tradition. He rebuked those who tithed their spices while neglecting justice, mercy, and faithfulness, the weightier matters of the law. He is the one who perfectly loves justice and shows mercy, and who by His Spirit replaces our hearts of stone with hearts of flesh, so that the justice and mercy God always wanted can finally flow from within.
basic.god: God searches the heart behind the ritual and is not fooled by outward religion. He cares intensely about how the weak are treated, the widow, the orphan, the foreigner, the poor. He is patient, sending prophet after prophet, but His anger is real, and hardened hearts bring judgment. Yet even His question invites the people to become what He always wanted them to be.
basic.crossReferences: Isaiah 58 exposes fasting without justice. Micah 6 asks what the LORD requires: justice, mercy, and humble walking. Matthew 23 rebuilds the weightier matters of the law. Ezekiel 36 promises a new heart of flesh in place of stone.
basic.oneStory: God redirects a question about fasting to the heart of true religion: justice and mercy from a soft heart. The hard hearts that ignored the prophets brought the exile; the call points forward to Christ, who fulfills mercy over sacrifice and gives His people new hearts by the Spirit, so that the justice God always desired can at last be lived.

context.literary:
Zechariah 7 opens a new half of the book, and it does so with a date. The text gives a formal date, 'the fourth year of King Darius,' and the word of the LORD comes in response to an actual question. The change of genre is deliberate. Chapters 1 to 6 show visions given to the prophet; chapters 7 and 8 record an exchange with real people about real practice. Chapter 7 is the long answer to a short question, and chapter 8 is its second half, which turns to promise. Verse 7:1 and 8:18-19 hold the pair like bookends: it begins with a question about the fast of the fifth month, and it ends with God announcing that the fasts of the fourth, fifth, seventh and tenth months will become 'times of joy and gladness, cheerful feasts.'

The answer to the question comes in a series of word-events, each opened by a formula. In 7:4 'the word of the LORD of Hosts came to me.' In 7:8 it comes again. Between them the argument runs in three steps. First God asks two questions that no one can answer comfortably, 7:5-6: was it for me, and was your eating not for yourselves? Then he reminds them that all of this had been said before, 7:7. Then he repeats the earlier message in four commands, 7:9-10, and recounts the refusal and its consequence, 7:11-14. The chapter moves from the present to the past, from a small inquiry to the history of the nation, and ends in the desolation of the land.

The phrase 'the earlier prophets' in 7:7 and 7:12 is the hinge of the argument. Zechariah's own book began with the same phrase, 'the former prophets,' who called the fathers to turn, 1:4-6. So the book comes full circle. The sermon of chapter 1 told the people not to be like their fathers, and chapter 7 shows exactly what their fathers did. The structure of the sermon is therefore a deliberate echo, and the people who asked about a fast are asked to listen to the message they had already heard. The sharpest line in the section is the reversal of 7:13: 'just as I had called and they would not listen, so when they called I would not listen.'
context.historical:
The date is the fourth day of the ninth month, Chislev, in Darius's fourth year, which falls in late 518 BC. Two years had passed since the visions, and the temple was about two years from completion. The delegation that came was sent, according to the BSB, by the people of Bethel, a town about twelve miles north of Jerusalem. Bethel had once been a major shrine, 1 Kings 12:28-29, and men of Bethel and Ai are among those who returned, Ezra 2:28. The footnote notes that the Hebrew can also be read as a personal name, Bethel-sharezer, who sent Regem-melech and his men. Either way the question was brought to the 'priests of the house of the LORD of Hosts' and to the prophets, because the temple was now the place to ask, even though it was not finished.

The fast at issue marked the destruction of the temple. According to Jeremiah 52:12 the Babylonian officer Nebuzaradan entered Jerusalem on the tenth day of the fifth month, and the temple was burned. The fast of the seventh month commemorated the murder of Gedaliah, the governor Babylon had left in charge, 2 Kings 25:25. The other two fasts mentioned in 8:19 look back to the siege that began on the tenth day of the tenth month and to the breach of the wall on the ninth day of the fourth month, Jeremiah 52:4-7. All four were remembered days of national disaster, and none of them was commanded by the Law. The Law's one prescribed day of self-denial is the Day of Atonement, when the people 'humble yourselves,' Leviticus 16:29-31. The four fasts had grown up in exile out of grief.

So the question was a natural one. The temple that the fast mourned was being rebuilt, and the people wondered whether the time of mourning was over. The words 'for these seventy years' in 7:5 give the length from the destruction in 586 BC to about 518, close to the seventy years of Jeremiah 29:10 and 2 Chronicles 36:21. Some of those who asked had kept the fast all their lives. The answer they received did not tell them whether to continue, and in that silence lay its first lesson: the real problem was not the calendar.
context.canonical:
The passage belongs to the great prophetic critique of worship divorced from justice. Isaiah 1:11-17 has God say he is full of burnt offerings, that he hates the appointed feasts, and that he will hide his eyes from outstretched hands that are 'covered with blood.' Amos 5:21-24 has him despise their feasts and call for justice to roll on like a river. Hosea 6:6 says, 'I desire mercy, not sacrifice,' and Micah 6:8 sums up what the LORD requires. Isaiah 58 is the closest parallel, because it concerns fasting itself. There the people ask why God has not noticed their fasts, and God says that on the day of the fast they oppress their workers, and that the fast he has chosen is to break chains, share bread and clothe the naked, Isaiah 58:3-7.

The reference to the fathers who would not listen draws on the covenant's own account of exile. Deuteronomy 28 had threatened scattering as the consequence of disobedience, and Zechariah 7:14 uses the vocabulary of that threat. The picture of the stubborn shoulder, the heavy ears and the heart like flint recalls Nehemiah 9:29, where the same posture of the fathers is confessed. The line 'they cried out and I would not listen' recalls Proverbs 1:24-28 and Jeremiah 11:11. The earlier prophets spoke 'by His Spirit,' as 7:12 says, so that the rejection of the prophets was a rejection of the Spirit who spoke through them.

The New Testament takes up the same themes. Jesus quotes Hosea 6:6 twice, in Matthew 9:13 and 12:7, and in Matthew 23:23 he tells the scribes and Pharisees that they pay tithes of mint, dill and cumin but have disregarded 'the weightier matters of the law: justice, mercy, and faithfulness.' Matthew 25:31-46 makes care for the hungry, the stranger and the prisoner the criterion of the last judgment. James 1:27 defines pure religion as caring for orphans and widows in their distress. Behind all of them is the answer given in Zechariah 7:9-10. It is also notable that Jesus does not abolish fasting: in Matthew 6:16-18 he assumes his disciples will fast, and in Matthew 9:15 he says they will when the bridegroom is taken from them.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
The answer Zechariah delivers was meant to unsettle a comfortable assumption, that a long and sincere observance puts God in the people's debt. By asking whether the fast was 'really for Me,' and then by turning to their eating and drinking, the prophet leaves no room for a reading in which fasting was holy and feasting was ordinary. In both, the question is whom they were serving. The comparison is meant to make the hearers see that they had treated the whole of life, mourning and celebration, as a performance for themselves.

He also meant to move them from the question of ritual to the matter of conduct. The four commands of 7:9-10 are not new. They are what the former prophets had said when the land was populous and prosperous. The returning community did not need a fresh word; they needed to recognise that the old word was still in force. The hearers are invited into the same decision that the fathers faced, and the second half of the chapter describes how it ended.

The review of the fathers' refusal is a warning that works as a mirror. The people of Judah could see exactly where unresponsive hearts lead: to a whirlwind, a scattering and a desolate land. Zechariah wanted his own generation, who had only just come back, to take hold of the possibility that history need not repeat itself. The following chapter shows why that hope is real: the God who scattered is the God who promises to return to Zion, 8:3.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
Two kinds of material run through the chapter, and they should be kept apart. Verses 9-10 are a prescription: administer true justice, show loving devotion and compassion, do not oppress the widow, the fatherless, the foreigner or the poor, and do not plot evil in your hearts. These are binding in every age because they express the character of God, who 'executes justice for the fatherless and widow,' Deuteronomy 10:18. Verses 11-14, in contrast, are description. They record what happened to the generation that refused, and the pattern warns but does not command.

The fasts themselves are the third kind of thing. They were a practice the people had adopted, not one God had set down in the Law, and the passage does not say they were wrong to keep them. It says that the practice had no value apart from the obedience God wanted. For Christians the application is not to abolish fasting, which Jesus assumed in Matthew 6:16-18 and the early church practised in Acts 13:2, but to examine its motive. Religious discipline is good when it is for God and when it flows out into justice. It is empty when it stands in place of it. Treating the harsh history of verses 13-14 as proof that every hardship is a punishment would go beyond the text, which speaks of a particular generation and a particular exile.

debates.question: Is God condemning fasting itself?

views.label: No, only the motive
views.case: God asks whether the fast was for him, and the answer implied is no. The problem is the self-serving nature of the practice. Chapter 8 then turns the fasts into feasts, so the fault was the heart and not the observance.

views.label: He places ritual under justice
views.case: Even a sincere fast has no standing before God if the weightier matters are neglected. Ritual is relativised and, when it replaces justice and mercy, it is worthless, though not forbidden.

debates.bearing: On both readings the lesson is the same: God wants the heart. Fasting that moves a person toward mercy for the needy is welcome, and fasting that leaves the oppressor unchanged is empty.

debates.question: Is Bethel a place or part of a name in verse 2?

views.label: The people of Bethel sent a delegation
views.case: The BSB reads that 'the people of Bethel had sent Sharezer and Regem-melech.' Bethel was a real town, and men of Bethel were among the returnees. A community asking about a ritual might send representatives to the temple.

views.label: Bethel-sharezer sent Regem-melech
views.case: The BSB footnote allows 'Bethel-sharezer had sent Regem-melech, along with his men.' On that reading the question comes from an individual of some standing, and Bethel is part of his name.

debates.bearing: The Hebrew is compact and can be read either way. The lesson of the passage does not depend on it, since in either case the question reaches the priests and the answer reaches the whole people of the land.

debates.question: Does 'I would not listen' close the door on repentance?

views.label: A settled judgment on that generation
views.case: Verse 13 states a measure-for-measure response: they would not listen, so when they called he would not listen. Jeremiah heard the same, Jeremiah 11:11, and the exile followed. The text is looking back at a generation that had already experienced it.

views.label: A principle with a door still open
views.case: Zechariah 1:3 gives the invitation, 'Return to Me, and I will return to you.' The record of what happened to the fathers is a warning, not a sentence on the present generation, so the passage should be read together with the call to return.

debates.bearing: Read within Zechariah, the past tense governs. God's refusal to hear belongs to that history, and the book as a whole holds the way back open to those who listen now.

study.originalLanguages:
The question in verse 3 is phrased in the first person singular: 'Should I weep and fast in the fifth month, as I have done these many years?' The 'I' is the voice of the individual worshipper, and it asks about his own long habit, yet the answer in verse 5 is addressed to 'all the people of the land and the priests,' so a private scruple is turned into a question for the whole community. God's reply uses the word tsum for fasting and adds a second verb, 'mourned,' from the root of the public lament. He names both halves of the practice, the abstaining and the weeping, and tests each.

God's own question has an emphatic shape. The BSB's 'was it really for Me that you fasted?' translates a Hebrew sentence that doubles the verb and then adds the pronoun for emphasis: tsom tsamtuni ani, roughly 'fasting, did you fast for me, for me?' The doubling is the intensive pattern Hebrew uses to stress an action, and the repeated pronoun makes the point twice. Verse 6 balances it by putting the pronoun 'you' before each verb, so that the Hebrew reads as you are the ones eating and you the ones drinking. The point is made twice, once for the fast and once for the feast.

The idiom in verse 2 is worth knowing. 'To plead before the LORD' is a phrase that literally means to make the face of the LORD sweet or soft, a Hebrew way of saying to entreat his favour. The same phrase appears in 8:21-22, when many peoples come 'to plead before the LORD.' So the section begins with a small delegation asking God to soften his face and ends with the nations doing the same thing. The inclusion links the question about a fast to the promise that the whole world will seek the LORD of Hosts in Jerusalem.

Verse 9 contains the chapter's positive demands, and its vocabulary is rich. 'True justice' is mishpat emet, literally justice of truth, judgment that corresponds to reality and not to the bribe or the status of the parties. 'Loving devotion' is chesed, which the BSB footnote at 7:9 explains covers love, goodness, kindness, faithfulness, mercy and loyalty to a covenant. 'Compassion' is rachamim, a word built from the Hebrew for the womb, so that mercy is the feeling of a mother for her child. The two are directed 'to one another,' which the Hebrew expresses as each man to his brother. Real religion takes the form of brotherly dealings.

The four classes in verse 10 are the standard group the Law calls the vulnerable: the widow, the fatherless, the foreigner (ger, the resident alien) and the poor. See Exodus 22:21-24 and Deuteronomy 10:18-19. The last command, 'do not plot evil in your hearts,' moves the issue inside, since the verb is the one for devising and the location is the heart. The same wording returns in 8:17.

The language of refusal in verses 11 and 12 is physical. 'A stubborn shoulder' is a shoulder that turns away and will not take the yoke, the image Nehemiah 9:29 also uses. The footnote at verse 11 says the Hebrew means 'they made their ears too heavy to hear.' The heart of flint is shamir, a word for an extremely hard stone, perhaps adamant, which Jeremiah 17:1 uses for the diamond point that engraves Judah's sin on the tablet of the heart. The fathers' hearts were harder than the stylus.

Finally, the desolation of verse 14. 'I scattered them with a whirlwind' uses a verb from the root for a storm wind. 'The pleasant land' is eretz chemdah, the 'desirable land,' from the root chamad, to desire. The same phrase appears in Psalm 106:24 and Jeremiah 3:19, where the people despised it. The last clause, 'they turned the pleasant land into a desolation,' puts the responsibility in the people's own hands. The land was desirable, and they made it a waste.

typology.type: The fast that the LORD chooses
typology.fulfillment: The prophets teach that the fast God wants is the release of the oppressed and the feeding of the hungry, Isaiah 58:6-7. In Jesus that fast takes flesh. He reads from Isaiah in the synagogue at Nazareth, 'He has sent Me to proclaim liberty to the captives... to release the oppressed,' Luke 4:18, and says that what is done for the least of his brothers is done for him, Matthew 25:40. The escalation is that justice and mercy are no longer only requirements to meet, but are shown in a person who feeds, heals and frees. The type falls short because Zechariah's commands remain demands on the hearers, while in Christ the demand is joined to power, the Spirit who writes the law on hearts, Jeremiah 31:33.

The hardened heart that will not hear pictures the state of humanity under sin, and the promise that answers it is the new heart: 'I will remove your heart of stone and give you a heart of flesh,' Ezekiel 36:26. In the New Testament this is the work of the Spirit, who writes God's law on the heart, 2 Corinthians 3:3, and in the new covenant that the blood of Christ secures, Hebrews 8:10. The escalation is from a diagnosis to a cure. The type falls short in that Zechariah's flint is a historical judgment on one generation, while the promise reaches every believer. The hardness of the fathers is also not wholly in the past, since the New Testament warns churches against hardening their hearts, Hebrews 3:7-8.

The ending of the chapter pair, in which the fasts of mourning become 'times of joy and gladness, cheerful feasts,' 8:19, points to the joy of the people of God when their sorrow is answered. Jesus speaks to this in Matthew 9:15, comparing his presence to a wedding where guests cannot mourn while the bridegroom is with them, and promising that the time will come when he will be taken, and then they will fast. The escalation is that mourning gives way to joy because the bridegroom has come, and joy reaches its fullness at the wedding supper of the Lamb, Revelation 19:7-9. The type falls short because Zechariah's feasts follow the rebuilding of one city, while Christ's joy follows the removal of sin and death.

study.christ:
Jesus stands where this passage points, and he does so first as the faithful speaker of the same word. When he says, 'I desire mercy, not sacrifice,' Matthew 9:13, he is quoting Hosea in answer to those who objected to his eating with sinners. When he turns on the scribes who tithe mint and cumin, he says they have neglected the weightier matters of the law, 'justice, mercy, and faithfulness,' Matthew 23:23. These are the same three commands that Zechariah 7:9 gives. The Lord who spoke to the exiles through the earlier prophets speaks in the Gospels in his own voice, and it is the same voice.

He is also the one who lived what Zechariah demanded. Where the fathers refused to hear, he listened: 'I do nothing on My own, but speak exactly what the Father has taught Me,' John 8:28. The worst the prophets could say of Israel was that they stopped their ears, and Isaiah's servant says, 'The Lord GOD has opened My ears, and I have not been rebellious,' Isaiah 50:5. The One who administers true justice, who showed compassion to the widow of Nain, Luke 7:11-15, who healed the servant of a Gentile centurion, Luke 7:1-10, and who cared for the poor, Luke 4:18, did exactly what chapter 7 required of Israel. He is the answer to the question 'was it really for Me?': everything he did was for the Father, John 4:34.

He is, thirdly, the means by which the hard heart is changed. The prophets named the flint, and Jesus gives the Spirit by whom the heart of stone is replaced. In Luke 4:18 he claims the anointing for 'good news to the poor,' and the Spirit's coming at Pentecost gives the new covenant's inward law, Ezekiel 36:26-27 and Jeremiah 31:33. A people who could not keep the commands of 7:9 from their own resources are given a heart that desires them. It is not that justice and mercy become unnecessary but that they are made possible.

There is also a note of judgment and of grace in the history of the fathers. The refusal to listen and the cry that was not heard recall the cry from the cross, 'My God, My God, why have You forsaken Me?' Matthew 27:46. The One who bore the silence that the fathers deserved did so in their place, so that those who call on him are heard. Hebrews 4:16 invites us to approach the throne of grace with confidence, because the door that Zechariah 7:13 describes as closed has been opened by his priesthood.

A caution is needed here. The chapter does not mention a Messiah, and the chapter does not need to. Its link to Christ is by continuity of word, by fulfilment of the demand, and by the cure of the heart. It should not be stretched to find hidden predictions in the delegation, the dates or the months. The plain force of the passage is enough: the one who stands behind it is the one who, as Hebrews 1:1-2 says, spoke to the fathers through the prophets and in these last days has spoken to us by his Son.
study.god:
The first thing the passage shows is a God who looks at the heart. The delegation's question concerned a calendar, and God's answer concerns a motive. He is not fooled by a long record of observance, and he is not impressed by sincerity of feeling when it has no fruit in how people treat each other. The question 'was it really for Me?' reveals a God who wants relationship and not performance. Worship, in his eyes, is not measured by hours or months but by whether it is directed to him and shown in a changed life.

He is also a God who cares about the vulnerable. The four categories of 7:10 are the people the Law returns to again and again, and God puts the widow, the orphan, the foreigner and the poor at the centre of what he requires. Deuteronomy 10:17-18 says that the God who shows no partiality and accepts no bribe 'executes justice for the fatherless and widow, and He loves the foreigner.' The God of Zechariah 7 is that God. Anything that claims to honour him while harming those he defends contradicts his character.

He is a God of patient speech. The word came through the earlier prophets, 'sent by His Spirit,' and came repeatedly. Judgment in this passage is the end of a long series of calls, not a sudden anger. The phrase 'just as I had called and they would not listen' shows that he did the calling first. The tragedy of the exile in this account is not that God was quick to punish but that he was slow, and that his people used his patience to harden themselves.

He is a God whose justice is exact. The refusal to listen was met with a refusal to listen, in the measure that matches it, and the scattering matches the scattering of those who were scattered. Yet the passage does not leave God as only a judge. He speaks in the same breath of his Spirit, his people and the pleasant land. The tone of 7:14 is grief as well as anger, since it is a land he called pleasant that was turned to a waste.

A tension runs through the chapter. God is deeply angry, and yet the section is the preface to a chapter in which he says, 'I will return to Zion and dwell in Jerusalem,' 8:3, and 'I will save My people,' 8:7. The same God holds both. His anger is real, but it is not his last word, and the prophets who spoke of exile also spoke of return. For worship this means that we come as people who have been told the truth about ourselves and about the cost of hardness, and who have also been told that the God who judged is the God who gathers. We bring our fasting, our singing and our offerings, and we bring them with open hands toward our neighbours.

crossReferences.note: The book's opening call: God was angry with the fathers, who did not listen to the former prophets. Chapter 7 returns to the same people and shows the detail behind that summary, so the two passages frame the first half of the book.

The answer to the original question arrives at last: the fasts of the fourth, fifth, seventh and tenth months become cheerful feasts, and the people are told to love truth and peace. Chapter 8 completes the argument chapter 7 begins.

The nearest parallel. People ask why God has not noticed their fasting, and he says they oppress their workers on the day of the fast. The fast he chooses is to break chains and share bread. It shows how long the prophets had made the same point.

God says he is tired of sacrifices and festivals, and calls the people to wash, to learn to do good and to defend the fatherless and widow. The pattern is the same: religious observance cannot stand in the place of justice.

'I hate, I despise your feasts!' and 'let justice roll on like a river.' Amos shows that the complaint about worship without justice goes back to the eighth century, long before the exile Zechariah's hearers remembered.

'I desire mercy, not sacrifice, and the knowledge of God rather than burnt offerings.' Jesus quotes this verse, so it is a bridge from Zechariah's question about fasting to the Gospels' picture of true religion.

The worshipper asks what to bring, burnt offerings or thousands of rams, and the answer is to act justly, love mercy and walk humbly. It answers the question 'what does God want from my ritual?' in the same terms as Zechariah.

God shows no partiality, defends the fatherless and widow, and loves the foreigner, so Israel must love the foreigner as well. It gives the theological ground for the four vulnerable groups of Zechariah 7:10.

The Levites confess that the fathers 'stubbornly shrugged their shoulders' and stiffened their necks. The identical gesture appears in Zechariah 7:11, so the returned community had already learned to describe this sin as its own history.

'If you act justly toward one another... if you no longer oppress the foreigner and the fatherless and the widow,' then God will let them live in the land. Jeremiah's temple sermon sets the same conditions as Zechariah 7:9-10 and ties them to the land itself.

Jesus says the scribes and Pharisees have 'disregarded the weightier matters of the law: justice, mercy, and faithfulness.' This repeats Zechariah's priorities and shows that the problem he described was not left behind in the exile.
God promises to remove the heart of stone, give a heart of flesh and put his Spirit within, to cause people to walk in his statutes. It is the cure for the flint heart of Zechariah 7:12.

study.oneStory:
The question about the fasts reaches into a theme that begins at the dawn of the Bible. In Genesis 4 Cain brings an offering and God asks about his heart, 'If you do what is right, will you not be accepted?' Genesis 4:7. From the start, worship has been tested by how people treat one another. Sinai gave the law of sacrifice and the law of the widow and the foreigner in the same covenant, and the prophets from Samuel to Malachi kept insisting on the second when the people kept the first. Zechariah 7 is one more voice in that chain, and its place is at the end, when the nation has already paid for ignoring the others.

Its setting is the turn from exile back to the land. The seventy years are ending, and the question is what kind of people will return. The chapter says that the only thing that matters is whether they will be what the fathers were not: listeners. That is why the section turns into the promise of chapter 8, where God returns to Zion and the city is called the City of Truth. The refusal that ended in a whirlwind is set against a promise of old men and women sitting in the streets and children playing, 8:4-5. The hope is that obedience will bring what disobedience lost.

The rest of the Bible tells how hard that obedience proves. The returned community builds the temple, yet Malachi still finds them cheating and Nehemiah still finds them oppressing, and the Gospels find a nation again full of ritual and light on mercy. The story needs a heart changed from within, and the New Testament proclaims that this has happened. The Spirit is poured out, the law written on the heart, and the people of Christ are told to carry the weightier matters of the law into the world, Matthew 23:23 and James 1:27. The church fasts, prays and gives, but its test is the one Zechariah announced.

The story ends in a city where the question has been answered. No one needs to ask whether a fast is for God, because the hardness is gone and the new heart is whole. 'Nothing unclean will ever enter it,' Revelation 21:27, and there is no mourning or crying or pain, Revelation 21:4. The feasts of Zechariah 8:19 become a wedding supper, Revelation 19:9, and the widow, the orphan, the foreigner and the poor are at the table. What the prophet demanded of one generation is given as the very life of a redeemed people.

quiz.q: How does God answer the question about whether to keep fasting?

options.text: He asks whether their fasting was ever truly for Him or only for themselves.
options.note: God probes the motive of the heart behind the ritual.

options.text: He gives a simple yes, keep fasting forever.
options.note: He redirects the question to the heart rather than giving a bare yes.

options.text: He forbids all fasting from now on.
options.note: He questions their motive, not the practice itself; chapter 8 turns fasts to feasts.

options.text: He refuses to answer at all.
options.note: He answers fully, redirecting them to justice and mercy.

quiz.q: What does God say He truly desires?

options.text: True justice, loving devotion, and compassion to one another.
options.note: Verses 9 and 10 summarize the message of the earlier prophets.

options.text: More frequent and longer fasts.
options.note: He wants justice and mercy, not increased ritual.

options.text: Larger sacrifices at the temple.
options.note: He prizes mercy over sacrifice, not bigger offerings.

options.text: Complete withdrawal from public life.
options.note: He calls for active justice and care for the vulnerable.

quiz.q: Whom does God specifically say not to oppress?

options.text: The widow, the fatherless, the foreigner, and the poor.
options.note: Verse 10 names the vulnerable God defends.

options.text: Only wealthy landowners.
options.note: His concern is the vulnerable, not the powerful.

options.text: Foreign kings and their armies.
options.note: The focus is the weak within the community, not foreign rulers.

options.text: No one in particular.
options.note: He names four vulnerable groups specifically.

quiz.q: Why did God scatter the earlier generation?

options.text: They made their hearts like flint and refused the prophets' call to justice.
options.note: Their hard-hearted refusal brought the exile, not neglected fasting.

options.text: They fasted too often.
options.note: The problem was refused justice, not excessive fasting.

options.text: They built the temple too quickly.
options.note: The issue was moral, a refusal to do justice and show mercy.

options.text: For no reason God gives.
options.note: God clearly names their hardness of heart as the cause.

quiz.q: How does this call point to Christ?

options.text: Jesus upholds mercy over sacrifice and gives new hearts by the Spirit to do justice.
options.note: He quotes I desire mercy and gives a heart of flesh in the new covenant.

options.text: Jesus abolished justice and mercy as outdated.
options.note: The opposite: He upholds them as the weightier matters of the law.

options.text: Jesus taught that ritual is all that matters.
options.note: He taught mercy and justice over empty ritual.

options.text: Jesus has no link to this passage.
options.note: He stands directly in this prophetic tradition.

questions: God asked whether their fasting was for Him or for themselves. Where might your own religious habits be quietly serving you rather than God?
God links true worship to justice for the widow, orphan, foreigner, and poor. Who are the vulnerable ones near you that God is calling you to defend?
The ancestors made their hearts like flint. Where do you sense your own heart hardening against something God has clearly said?
God desires loving devotion and compassion, not just correct ritual. How could you show warm-hearted mercy to someone this week rather than mere duty?
Christ gives a new heart of flesh by His Spirit. Where do you need Him to soften and renew your heart so that justice and mercy flow naturally?

translationNotes.note: The fifth-month fast mourned the burning of the temple; the seventh-month fast in verse 5 mourned the murder of Gedaliah, both events of Jerusalem's fall.

Loving devotion renders chesed, whose range includes love, goodness, kindness, faithfulness, mercy, and covenant loyalty; justice renders mishpat, the right ordering of society that protects the weak.
Stopped up their ears is literally they made their ears too heavy to hear, a vivid image of willful deafness paired with hearts of flint in verse 12.
